source.version: Journal version of record: Science Advances 10, eadn5290 (2024), published 12 July 2024 (submitted 14 December 2023, accepted 7 June 2024), DOI 10.1126/sciadv.adn5290; downloaded from science.org on May 27, 2026. The PDF holds the 9-page article plus a cover page; the Supplementary Materials (sections S1 to S9, tables S1 to S18, figs. S1 to S6) are not in this PDF.
source.title_on_document: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content

paper_design_summary: In a preregistered online experiment on Prolific (UK), 293 writers were randomly assigned to write an eight-sentence story with no AI (Human-only), with the option to request one GPT-4 three-sentence story idea, or with the option to request up to five such ideas. A separate group of 600 evaluators rated six stories each (3,519 evaluations) for novelty, usefulness, and emotional characteristics, and the authors computed embedding cosine similarity of each story to the other stories in its condition and to a GPT-4 idea.

studies.label: Writer experiment (short-story writing with optional GPT-4 story ideas) plus evaluator rating study

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing condition: Human-only, Human with one GenAI idea (option to request one GPT-4 three-sentence story idea), or Human with five GenAI ideas (option to request up to five). Story topic (open seas, jungle, different planet) was also randomized.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: Humanonly, Human with one GenAI idea condition, and Human with five GenAI ideas (see table S1 for balance across conditions).
assignment.locator: p. 2, Results preamble (first paragraph, left column); also p. 7, Materials and Methods, 'Writer study and experimental conditions'
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 8, 'Preregistration and ethics approval': AsPredicted.org ID 136723 (copy in supplementary section S9, not in this PDF)

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Writers wrote the story with no mention of or access to generative AI.

arms.name: Human with one GenAI idea
arms.description: Writers could click 'Generate Story Idea' once to receive a three-sentence GPT-4 story idea; they could not copy and paste it. 82 of 100 requested an idea (p. 2).

arms.name: Human with five GenAI ideas
arms.description: Writers could request up to five three-sentence GPT-4 story ideas, all visible; no copy and paste. 93 of 98 requested at least one; mean 2.55 requests; 24.5% requested all five (p. 2).

participants.exclusions: Of 500 Prolific participants who began, 169 exited before consent, 22 were dropped for not giving consent, 13 dropped out before completing, and 3 Human-only writers who admitted using generative AI were dropped per the preregistration, leaving 293 writers and 293 stories (p. 7). DAT score computed for 291 of 293 writers (p. 3). The paper does not state how many were randomized or the analyzed count of the Human-only arm (the 100 and 98 for the AI arms are on p. 2). Separately, 600 evaluators (not randomized to AI) produced 3,519 evaluations; evaluations of dropped writers' stories were removed (pp. 7-8).
participants.who: Prolific participants based in the United Kingdom with an approval rating of at least 95 percent over 100 to 1,000,000 prior submissions, not selected on writing skill or creativity. Evaluators: a separate set of 600 Prolific UK participants who had not taken part in the writer study.
participants.quote: Three participants in the Human-only condition admitted to using generative AI during their story writing exercise and—as per our preregistration—were therefore dropped from the analysis, resulting in a total number of writers and stories of 293.
participants.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, 'Writer study and experimental conditions'; arm counts p. 2, 'Baseline versus generative AI conditions'; evaluators p. 2 and p. 8

ai_tool.how_used: On request, the interface sent the fixed prompt 'Write a three-sentence summary of a story about [topic]' to GPT-4 and showed the reply. Writers could not customize the prompt, interact further, or copy and paste the idea (p. 7; p. 6). Analysis is intention-to-treat by assigned condition (p. 6).

task.description: Write a story of exactly eight sentences in English on a randomly assigned topic (an adventure on the open seas, in the jungle, or on a different planet), appropriate for a teenage and young adult audience (about 15 to 24 years); 'You can write about anything you like.' No financial incentives for performance.

outcomes.name: Novelty index (evaluator-rated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean of three 9-point items (novel, original, rare) rated by Prolific evaluators blind to condition; Cronbach's alpha 0.92 (p. 8). OLS on evaluations with condition dummies, robust SEs clustered by evaluator (p. 8); results qualitatively unchanged with evaluator, story-order, and topic fixed effects and an AI-use indicator (table S4, p. 3). Component items shown in Fig. 2A.

contrasts.locator: p. 3, Results, first paragraph; Fig. 2A (p. 3); table S3 (supplement, not in this PDF)

contrasts.locator: p. 3, Results, first paragraph; Fig. 2A (p. 3); table S3 (supplement, not in this PDF)

outcomes.name: Similarity of story to other stories in the same condition (embedding cosine similarity)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity x 100 (0 to 100) between the focal story's embedding and the average embedding of all other stories in the same condition; embeddings from OpenAI's embeddings API (pp. 4, 8). Higher means more similar, so the sign is reversed relative to diversity. Fig. 4A shows kernel densities; Fig. 4B the coefficients.

contrasts.reported: more similar to the average of other stories within the same condition (Human with one GenAI idea condition: b = 0.871, P < 0.001 ... see table S11); 10.7% of the 8.10-point range of similarity scores in the Human-only condition. Direction coded for diversity (similarity higher, diversity lower).
contrasts.locator: p. 4, 'Similarity of stories', second paragraph; Fig. 4B (p. 5); table S11 (supplement)

contrasts.reported: Human with five GenAI ideas condition: b = 0.718, P = 0.003, see table S11; 8.9% of the 8.10-point Human-only range. Direction coded for diversity (similarity higher, diversity lower).
contrasts.locator: p. 4, 'Similarity of stories', second paragraph; Fig. 4B (p. 5); table S11 (supplement)

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of story embeddings, multiplied by 100
diversity_detail.embedding_model: OpenAI embeddings API (specific model not named)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each story against the centroid (average embedding) of all other stories in the same condition
diversity_detail.uncertainty: OLS of story-level similarity on condition dummies with robust standard errors (writer-study outcome, one story per writer; p. 8)
diversity_detail.notes: The leave-one-out centroid is computed within condition, so each story's score depends on the other stories in its own arm. Arm-level means and SDs are not printed in the main text.

outcomes.name: Similarity of story to a GPT-4 story idea (anchoring)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity x 100 between the story embedding and a GenAI idea: the first idea received for writers who used AI; for Human-only writers and AI-arm writers who requested none, an idea drawn at random from the pool of ideas generated for other writers on the same topic (pp. 5, 8). Mechanism measure of anchoring on the AI idea, not a creativity or across-people diversity measure.

outcomes.name: Writer self-assessed novelty, usefulness, and story characteristics
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Writers rated their own story's novelty and usefulness (9-point scale) and six stylistic statements after writing (p. 7). Self-report; does not meet criterion 3. Tables S5 and S7.

company_involvement.description: No company staff among authors; funding from the University of Exeter Business School and UCL School of Management; authors declare no competing interests. GPT-4 was accessed through the OpenAI API as the study's tool only.

eligibility.reason: Writers were randomly assigned to no AI or to the option of one or up to five GPT-4 story ideas (p. 2, p. 7); 293 writers analyzed, 100 and 98 in the two AI arms (pp. 2, 7); outcomes are novelty and usefulness rated by blind evaluators and embedding similarity across stories within condition (pp. 3-4, 8).

one_line_finding: Relative to Human-only, the option of up to five GPT-4 story ideas raised evaluator-rated novelty (b = 0.311, P < 0.001) and usefulness (b = 0.453, P < 0.001) (p. 3), while stories in both AI arms were more similar to the other stories in their condition (one idea b = 0.871, P < 0.001; five ideas b = 0.718, P = 0.003) (p. 4).
open_questions: The analyzed count of the Human-only arm is not printed; 293 total minus 100 and 98 implies 95, but the paper does not state it. Per-arm randomized counts are not given.

Standard errors, arm means, and SDs are in supplementary tables S3, S4, S6, S11 and section S4, which are not in this PDF. The main text prints only coefficients, P values, and percentage changes; Fig. 2 and Fig. 4B plot the coefficients with intervals on an axis labeled 'Effect size'.

Evaluator-rated outcomes are estimated on 3,519 evaluations with SEs clustered by evaluator, not by writer (the randomized unit); under codebook section 10 these SEs may not qualify for pooling without a writer-level reanalysis (data are posted on Dryad).
Whether the similarity-to-other-stories outcome was preregistered is not stated in the main text; the preregistered indices named are novelty and usefulness.
Under codebook rule 8.3 the five-ideas arm is probably closer to free chatbot use than the one-idea arm, but neither arm allows open chat; the reviewer should choose the primary contrast.
AI use was optional within the AI arms (82 of 100 and 93 of 98 requested ideas); estimates are intention-to-treat.
notes: The PDF is the journal article only (9 pages plus a Science Advances cover page); all supplementary sections and tables cited in the text are absent. Heterogeneity by the writer's DAT score (pre-treatment Divergent Association Task, mean 77.24, SD 6.48) is reported in tables S9-S10 and Fig. 3: among low-DAT writers, one idea raised novelty by 6.3 percent and five ideas by 10.7 percent, usefulness by 5.5 and 11.5 percent (p. 4). Evaluator outcomes on authorship, ownership, profit shares, and AI ethics (section S5) are perceptions, not creativity scores, and are not listed. Percent changes are as printed by the authors; the axis on Fig. 2 and Fig. 4B is labeled 'Effect size' but the plotted points appear to match the raw b coefficients in the text (e.g., novelty 0.207 and 0.311).
